name: Agents (aiwaves)
description: Python framework for multi-agent language pipelines (SOP graphs of nodes and agents) with symbolic-learning optimizers that rewrite prompts and pipelines.
scored_configuration: Solution(SolutionConfig(<json>)).run() with default constructor arguments; tools only as listed in the config, with the shipped chatbot example (which enables code_interpreter) used where the framework rules call for official usage.
headline: This framework executes model tool calls immediately with no approval, validation, sandbox, or run limit. Its flagship code-interpreter tool runs Open Interpreter on the host as your user, with your OpenAI key, so a hijacked or runaway agent has your whole machine. Importing it also loads a .env file and passes two environment values to Python eval, and persisted artifacts do not protect the API key. Treat it as research code, not something to run on untrusted input.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: The framework has no agent identity or authorization layer. Every agent and tool runs with the developer's OS user and environment; the code-interpreter tool hands Open Interpreter the OPENAI_API_KEY and runs it in-process with full access to the host. Nothing narrows what a hijacked agent can reach.

S.finding: Ambient authority only: the OpenAI key is read from the process environment and the code interpreter runs as the OS user.
S.gap: No dedicated or scoped identity for agents or tools.

evidence.note: hits are Apache license headers and Gmail OAuth SCOPES in the unregistered mail tool; no authorization layer

C.finding: The tool executor calls tool.func directly with no authorization check.
C.gap: No authorization check on the main tool path.

D.finding: Defaults use the operator's full environment; no least-privilege option exists.
D.gap: No narrower default identity exists to enable.

B.gap: Nothing confines tools below the OS user's authority.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: There is no approval step anywhere. The agent loop parses the model's tool call and executes it immediately, including the code interpreter that writes and runs arbitrary code. The framework offers no hook for a human to review or reject a call, so every consequential action is unattended.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Tools receive the model's arguments with no validation in code: the JSON arguments are splatted straight into the tool function. The built-in tools are general-purpose (free-form code requests, sympy expressions that sympify evaluates). The one real narrowing is that toolkits are built only from named entries in a fixed registry and the agent rejects tool names it was not given.

S.finding: Raw passthrough: arguments go straight from json.loads to tool.func, and the main tool accepts a free-form coding request.
S.gap: No typed validation, allowlists, or bounds on tool arguments.

C.gap: No tool or shared layer validates arguments.

D.finding: Agents get no tools unless the config lists them, and only names in AVAILABLE_TOOLS can be built; but the registry's flagship tool is unrestricted code execution and the chatbot example enables it.
D.gap: No read-only default set or per-task tool allowlists beyond the config; capped one level above S.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Model-influenced code runs without isolation on several paths: the code-interpreter tool runs Open Interpreter on the host, the math tools pass model strings to sympy's eval-based parser, and two settings read from environment variables are passed to Python eval. The HumanEval scorer runs generated code in a subprocess with a function-disabling guard whose own docstring says it is not a security sandbox. Nothing contains an escape, and the host process holds the API key.

S.finding: The main execution path (Open Interpreter) runs on the host as the same user; the only other mechanism is an in-process function-nulling guard explicitly documented as not a sandbox.
S.gap: No OS-level separation (container, low-privilege user) for any execution path.

evidence.note: hits are Azure storage-container docstrings and the reliability_guard disclaimer that it is not a sandbox

C.gap: The main exec tool is not behind any boundary.

D.finding: No sandbox exists to be on by default.
D.gap: No isolation available even as an option.

evidence.note: hits are Azure storage-container docstrings and the reliability_guard disclaimer that it is not a sandbox

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Nothing separates untrusted content from instructions. Peer agents' messages are folded into a user-role observation, tool results become the agent's next content, and retrieved knowledge-base or memory text goes straight into prompts. With the code interpreter enabled, a hijacked agent can both exfiltrate data and take irreversible actions with no human involved.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: No structural limit on a hijacked agent; there is not even a delimiter or classifier.
S.gap: No approval or capability restriction after untrusted content is read.

C.finding: Tool results, peer messages, and retrieved memory enter context with the same standing as instructions.
C.gap: Untrusted sources are not distinguished at all.

D.finding: No control exists to be on by default.
D.gap: No control to enable.

B.finding: With the code interpreter (chatbot example) a hijacked agent can read secrets, send them anywhere, and modify the host unattended.
B.gap: Some leg of the Rule of Two must be removed or gated in code.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Agent and shared environment long-term memory are appended to JSONL files under a relative memory/ directory that is never cleared, so content from one run persists into the next and is retrieved into routing prompts when a knowledge base is configured. The LLM module calls load_dotenv() at import, so a .env file found by python-dotenv's search can redirect the model endpoint and key, and two settings from the environment are passed to Python eval, turning a planted .env into code execution. There is no validation, provenance, or isolation on any of it.

cap.reason: load_dotenv() runs at import (llm.py:27) and the code then reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and evals TOP_K/ENVIRONMENT_SUMMARY_STEP from the environment; python-dotenv's default find_dotenv walks up from the calling file's directory, so a .env in the project tree (e.g. a project-local venv or editable install) silently redirects the model endpoint or executes code (library behaviour inferred).

S.finding: Model output is appended to persistent memory unvalidated, and an auto-loaded .env can redirect OPENAI_BASE_URL and inject code via eval of TOP_K / ENVIRONMENT_SUMMARY_STEP.
S.gap: No validation or provenance on memory writes; environment files load silently.

C.finding: No memory store or auto-loaded file is controlled.
C.gap: No store or config path is controlled.

D.finding: Memory paths are fixed relative files (memory/<agent>.jsonl, memory/environment.jsonl) shared by every run in the same directory.
D.gap: No per-user or per-session namespace.

B.finding: Poisoned memory persists across runs and is retrieved into the transit prompt that picks the next node and acting agent.
B.gap: Persistent memory is not confined to text output or gated actions.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: The only record is a JSON dump of the prompt messages and the final content, written to a relative logs/ directory when a tool is called (and on other calls only if SAVE_LOGS is set). It does not record which tool ran or with what arguments, and the logger deletes all but the newest 20 files in the directory. Training mode keeps fuller trajectories, but normal runs leave no reliable audit trail.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: A run has no limit on steps, time, or cost. Solution.run loops until the SOP reaches its end node; the per-node max_chat_nums check is overwritten by the LLM or order transition on the next line, single-successor nodes loop forever, and the LLM call retries forever on errors. Only the training loop (max_step) and the HumanEval scorer (3-second timeout with process kill) are bounded.

S.finding: No enforced step, time, or cost limit on a run; the only cap (max_chat_nums) is dead code and retries are infinite.
S.gap: No iteration cap that actually stops a run.

evidence.note: all hits are in the HumanEval evaluator and its time_limit helper; nothing bounds the agent run loop

C.finding: Limits apply to nothing in the agent loop.
C.gap: No limit covers the top-level loop.

D.gap: No default limit exists.

B.gap: No ceiling on spend or time.

critical_findings.summary: The registered code_interpreter tool runs Open Interpreter on the host as the OS user with the API key, so a hijacked agent holds the user's full local authority.
Model-written code (code_interpreter, sympify, eval of env vars) executes on the host with the user's files, network, and API key; the only guard is documented as not a sandbox.
A hijacked agent with the code interpreter can leak secrets and take irreversible host actions with no human in the loop (C5-WORSTCASE).
load_dotenv() at import plus eval() of environment values lets a planted .env redirect the model endpoint or run arbitrary Python, with no trust decision (C6-REPOCONFIG).
Packages installed at the model's request through the code interpreter run as the user with the full environment and API key.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: peer/tool/retrieved content enters prompts unmarked (src/agents/agents/agent.py:134-141, src/agents/task/sop.py:418)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: OPENAI_API_KEY in process env and passed to the interpreter (src/agents/tools/code_interpreter.py:25-27)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: code_interpreter runs arbitrary code with network on the host (src/agents/tools/code_interpreter.py:34)

fixes.summary: Enforce a hard step/wall-clock cap in Solution.run, fix the overwritten max_chat_nums branch, and bound LLM retries.
Add an approval callback in Agent.step before tool.func showing the exact tool name and arguments, on by default for code_interpreter.
Drop the import-time load_dotenv() and replace eval() of environment values with int().
Keep credentials out of persisted artifacts and redact secrets from saved logs and trajectories.
Run the code interpreter in a hardened container with a scrubbed environment by default.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
Open Interpreter 0.2.5 behaviour (no confirmation when called programmatically via chat(display=False), ability to pip install) is inferred from that library, not read in this repo.
python-dotenv find_dotenv search behaviour (walks up from the calling file's directory) is inferred from the library.

Unregistered tools (web_search, web_crawl, mail, translate, weather) are importable but not reachable via Toolkit config; reviewed but not scored as defaults. Datasets under src/agents/datasets/data were not read.
No text aimed at AI reviewers was found (searched for auditor/AI-reviewer phrasing).
